A/HI 201: Chado allows a glimpse of Japanese culture from the perspective of a variety of different artistic media and a long historic tradition. The course will focus on the background of the Way of Tea, Zen and Japanese aesthetics and learning the most basic tea procedure. Through this course, students will gain insight into the many arts and crafts, architecture styles, Japanese aesthetic values, literature and the importance of the seasons associated with Chado as well as basic Japanese customs.
A/HI 202: This course continues a study of Japanese culture from the perspective of a variety of different artistic media and delves deeper into the history and context surrounding the evolution of the Way of Tea. It expands the student's understanding of the Japanese appreciation of utensils: their form, function and beauty; excellence in craftsmanship; and the practice of ''copying.'' Repeatable up to six credits including original course. Can only be used for GUR credit once.
A/HI 210: History of Architecture: Prehistory to Modernity.
A/HI 211: This course examines Western art from Prehistory to the Middle Ages, concentrating on representative works that shaped — and were shaped by — Western culture’s social, political, economic, and intellectual history. There will be a strong emphasis, too, on questions of visual analysis and interpretation. The goal is to impart not only a body of art historical knowledge but also a set of critical tools and visual literacy. The visual and aesthetic core aspects of the course will be further elucidated with primary sources and documentaries.
A/HI 212: This course examines Western art from the Renaissance to modernity, concentrating on representative works that shaped — and were shaped by — Western culture’s social, political, economic, and intellectual history.
A/HI 240: Issues and topics in art, 19th century.
A/HI 241: Issues and topics in art, 20th century.
A/HI 245: Introductory survey of African American art from the 18th century to the present, primarily within the United States.
A/HI 250: An introduction to key issues and themes in African art from prehistoric rock art to the implementation of colonial rule. Case studies include brasscasting, sculpture, masquerade, textiles, and photography. Specifically, the course will explore how these traditions express various aspects of human experience, and how these traditions change over the course of history.
A/HI 251: Introduction to key issues and themes in African art from 1900 to the present, including the entire continent and its diaspora. Through these local and global traditions, the problems of human existence are communicated and problematized before, during, and after colonialism.
A/HI 261: This course introduces students to the richness and vast production of art, architecture, and visual culture of Latin America after 1900. The course covers formative movements and approaches to the visual field, emphasizing late 19th century uprisings against colonial rule before focusing on the 20th and 21st centuries. Students will learn how artists contended with shifting perspectives on race, class, and gender, alongside their relationships to national political movements and European avant-gardes. We will trace the emergence of Chicanx and Latine artistic practices in the postwar United States, as American artists further established concepts around identity. Finally, the course analyzes a vast array of practices, using artist statements, manifestos, and secondary texts to comprehend the dynamic production of such communities throughout the Americas.
A/HI 270: Issues and topics in South and Southeast Asian art and visual culture, from ancient to contemporary.
A/HI 271: Issues and topics in Chinese, Korean, and Japanese visual culture, from ancient to contemporary. Also offered as EAST 271.
A/HI 272: This course will examine contemporary visual practices in Asia, considering both continuing historical as well as entirely novel art genres and media. It will introduce artists who are responding to their contemporary environment in a variety of innovative ways. Through image analysis and discussion of reading material, artistic forms will be explored and discussed with consideration of the social, political, religious and economic contexts within which they were made and within a broader global context.
A/HI 297: Introduction to key issues and themes in African art from 1900 to the present, including the entire continent and its diaspora. Through these local and global traditions, the problems of human existence are communicated and problematized before, during, and after colonialism.
A/HI 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
A/HI 301: Survey and critical analysis of modernist, theory and criticism.
A/HI 302: Assist faculty in the classroom and with activities such as lecture preparation, class website upkeep, classroom discussion, research, and reviews for exams. Duties vary by course and instructor, but the time commitment will be 3-9 hours/week.
A/HI 305: Emphasis on art preparation/installation methods, gallery/collections management, and museum education/public programming. Students must commit to registering for this class for fall, winter and spring quarter. Repeatable to a maximum of 9 credits, including original course. Intended as a resume building class. Credits may not be used for the Art History major or minor.
A/HI 306: Internship at museum, educational or public arts organization under the direction of a designated art history faculty member, in consultation with a staff member of the host institution. Intended as a resume building class. Credits may not be used for the art history major or minor. Repeatable to a maximum of 9 credits, including original course.
A/HI 308: A hands-on class designed to give students a practical experience in promotion of visual culture in the community.
A/HI 310: Selected topics in the arts of the Pacific Northwest. Includes discussion of contemporary artists.
A/HI 313: Critical approaches to the study of artistic practices based on visual technology. Topics may include: photography, film, video, computer-generated art and electronic media.
A/HI 316: Studies of landscape and ideology in painting and garden design; issues of environment in the production of visual culture; relationships of land and architecture.
A/HI 317: An advanced lecture on late Renaissance and Baroque in Europe.
A/HI 318: This advanced lecture studies two centuries of artistic production and aesthetic ideas, exploring Rococo, Neoclassicism, Romanticism, Realism, Impressionism, and Post-Impressionism.
A/HI 330: The ideological basis of painting, sculpture and manuscript illumination as tools of communication. The interdependence of textual and visual traditions and their subversion or alteration.
A/HI 335: This course explores artistic responses to the unprecedented clash and integration of cultures resulting from exploration and the consequent expansion of European empires throughout the world in its earliest phase, ca. 1492 to 1700.
A/HI 337: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
A/HI 348: This cross-disciplinary course examines how our natural environment is conceptualized in art, science and media. Through lectures, collaborative projects and experiential learning, students engage with historic debates associated with discoveries in natural science and current controversies on climate change, ecology and biodiversity.
A/HI 358: Examines postwar American culture, from 1950 to 1970, and critically assesses the relationships between art, popular media and the social upheavals of the postwar era.
A/HI 360: Studies in the relationship between ideas of nation and the formation of cultural identity.
A/HI 368: Art of Melanesia, Polynesia, Micronesia. Includes study of contemporary Pacific arts.
A/HI 370: Topics addressing historical and contemporary Islamic visual cultures in the Middle East, Africa, and Asia.
A/HI 371: Study of visual cultures in Japan from 5000 BCE to present. Analysis of cultural influx and assimilation from Asia and Europe as well as indigenous and individual visual expressions. Also offered as EAST 371.
A/HI 372: This course will examine film practice in one or more Asian countries with an emphasis on narrative construction and stylistic techniques. Repeatable to a maximum of 10 credits under different topics, including original course.
A/HI 375: Methodological approaches to the study of Art History and further development of writing skills and visual analysis.
A/HI 381: This course explores the ways in which African art confirms, legitimizes, and challenges authority on a local, national, and global level.
A/HI 383: This course explores the creative practices of artists of African descent who live and work beyond the continent, from World War II to the present.
A/HI 385: This course explores the creative practices and primary themes of African film directors, both on the continent and in the diaspora.
A/HI 388: This course will address the history and theory of museums, while simultaneously introducing students to contemporary museum practices and various aspects of museum work. In addition to critically examining the development of the institution of the museum in the United States, the course will also consider the ways societies have collected, classified, and displayed knowledge and material culture throughout time. Through readings, discussions and sessions with museum professionals, students will gain knowledge and understanding of the nature of museums, the work that they do, and the dynamics at play, both within the institution and within their larger communities.
A/HI 391: Advanced lecture course focused on specialized topics in the history of art. Repeatable with different topics to a maximum of 15 credits, including the original course.
A/HI 396: Study traditional and contemporary culture in Japan. Activities include: visiting historical sites, galleries, museums and artist studios. Experience a tea ceremony, papermaking, weaving, natural dyeing and more. Students will write a paper following the trip. Offered summer quarter only.
A/HI 397A: Combined Art/Art History course. On-site study of both traditional/contemporary Japanese culture. Visual presentation or art exhibition through their trip. Visiting historical sites, galleries and museums. Viewing dyeing/weaving/paper making/ceramic studios. Experiencing Gion Matsuri (the most famous summer festival in Kyoto), tea ceremony, papermaking and more. Summer only.
A/HI 397B: A/HI mjrs: A/HI 275; non-mjrs: 9 cr A/HI
A/HI 397C: Combined Art/Art History course. On-site study of both traditional and contemporary Japanese culture. Visual presentation or art exhibition through thier trip. Visiting historical sites, galleries and museums. Viewing dyeing/weaving/papermaking, and ceramics studios. Experience the Gion Festival (the most famous summer festival in Kyoto), a tea ceremony, papermaking, natural dyeing, and more. Summer only.
A/HI 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
A/HI 401: Theoretical analysis of late twentieth century postmodernist art and culture, and critical discussion of the expansion of visual media during the contemporary era.
A/HI 411: Examines Japanese artistic forms and visual culture from Post-World War II until the present. Explores connections between Japanese socioeconomic and artistic developments, as well as visual manifestations of contemporary Japanese youth culture. Topics include anime, manga, Harajuku fashion and art movements such as Gutai and Superflat. Also offered as EAST 411.
A/HI 413: Theoretical and cultural analysis of the history of representing space within Western art and architecture, from Gothic cathedrals and Renaissance perspective to cubist fractured surfaces and contemporary heterogeneous space.
A/HI 415: Topics in urban organization, urban/rural dynamics, regionalism, spaces and social production in the built environment and the arts.
A/HI 430: This seminar focuses on Western sacred artworks and theological aesthetic theories. Topics may include, amongst others: devotional images, popular images, the educational role of images in liturgy, pilgrimage churches, reliquaries, the performativity of icons, or the effects of the Protest and reformation and subsequent Catholic reformation.
A/HI 431: Studies in topics such as collecting, pilgrimage, touring and acquisition of the authentic.
A/HI 434: This seminar presents a study of 18th-Century art and culture in the Western world. Topics include: pictorial and philosophical conceptualizations of freedom; artistic defenses and challenges to the Academy; fashion and identity; the birth of art criticism; portraiture as political performativity.
A/HI 437: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
A/HI 438: Studies past and present visual practices, and how they engage with cultural representations of gender, sex, and sexuality, along with their interconnections to class and race. Course topics may include self-fashioning and performativity, portraiture and identity, patronage and matronage, the body as political, intersectionality, women painters in the Academy, feminism and femininity, nuns as divine artists, queer theory, and/or transgender and gender non-conforming artists. Specific geographic areas and time periods covered in the course may vary.
A/HI 440: Theoretical and critical approaches to the development of cyberspace and its relationship to new media, electronic art, virtual reality, videogames, and biotech art.
A/HI 445: This course will focus on the artistic domain of the diaspora, defined as a people dispersed from their homeland, and/or the new territory they and their descendants occupy. Historical circumstances of exile, migration, and movement will act as context for the art and culture under study. The significance of national, racial, ethnic, religious, and other identities upon these will be considered. Repeatable with different topics to a maximum of 15 credits, including original course.
A/HI 446: A seminar on aesthetics and art theory. Possible topics may include: definitions of art; Renaissance theories of perspective; Romanticism and the sublime; theories of viewership; phenomenology; post-structuralism; critical theory.
A/HI 447: This course presents a study of core questions framing the encounter between artists and the public sphere, exploring the moral, civic, and legal status and responsibilities of artists in relationship to political authorities, legal systems, and the art market.
A/HI 450: Analysis of how visual culture has been colonized and, increasingly, decolonized, with a focus on how power dynamics operate through visual forms. Readings focus on specific examples, with postcolonial theory, critical race theory, and queer theory providing frameworks for students to build their own analyses.
A/HI 451: This course focuses on the textiles arts of the African continent and its diaspora, which have been historically overlooked and underappreciated in Western academia. In this course we will give the textile arts careful and detailed study not just for their formal properties and technical achievements, but for the economic, social, political, religious, performative, and other roles they play in the communities that make and use them.
A/HI 489: Examines museum architecture and the exhibition of architecture in museums in Europe and America from the eighteenth century to the present.
A/HI 490: Seminar on issues such as the display of visual experience and the configuration of public culture and community identities by artists, institutions and audiences. Repeatable to a maximum of 10 credits, including original course.
A/HI 491: In-depth seminar course on a specific topic. Repeatable with different topics to a maximum of 15 credits, including the original course.
A/HI 497E: This advanced seminar will introduce participants to various ways one might experience and analyze built environments to better understand the production, development, and use of the architectures around and in which we live. Topics considered will include point of view, scale, function, history, memory and preservation. Examples will be drawn from historical and local/regional contexts.
A/HI 497R: A seminar exploring sacred artworks and their corresponding aesthetic, cultural, social or theological theories. Topics explored in the course may include: depictions of religious events, sacred spaces, miraculous images, popular cult images, iconoclasm, and other relevant topics. Repeatable to 10 credits with different topics, including original course.
ACCT 175: Introduction to the taxation of individuals and sole proprietorships. The course includes a practicum component that requires engaging with income-qualifying and retired taxpayers to file their annual tax returns.
ACCT 240: An introduction to the theory and practice of accounting and financial reporting. Topics include the accounting cycle, financial statements and accounting for assets, liabilities, equities, revenues and expenses.
ACCT 245: An introduction to the use of accounting information by managers. Topics include the use of accounting information for planning and control, performance evaluation, and decision-making.
ACCT 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ACCT 321: An introduction to the subject of information system's role in accomplishing the objectives of financial accounting, managerial accounting, and auditing. Topics include advanced Excel use, enterprise systems, risk management, internal controls, systems analysis and documentation, and project management.
ACCT 331: Procedures used for classifying, recording, summarizing and allocating current, and estimated costs for planning, controlling and reporting purposes.
ACCT 337: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
ACCT 341: An in-depth study of accounting theory and practice for students who require more than introductory coverage. Both conceptual and application topics are studied.
ACCT 342: A continuation of ACCT 341 covering complex topics in accounting and financial reporting.
ACCT 343: A continuation of ACCT 342 covering complex topics in accounting and financial reporting. Special topics, existing and emerging issues in accounting.
ACCT 375: An introduction to the tax environment, the role of income taxes in decision making, the basics of business taxation, and the tax research process (including communication).
ACCT 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ACCT 421: Principles and techniques of accounting analytics will be covered. Topics include sources and uses of multiple types of business data, data visualization, and reporting and analysis for decision making. A wide variety of technology tools will be used.
ACCT 422: Topics covered include the ability to configure an enterprise system and use the system for problem analysis, report generation, and data extraction and importation. Spreadsheets will be developed and analyzed for problem analysis, reporting, and trouble shooting. Accounting, MIS students are allowed to take both ACCT 422 and ACCT 421 for elective credit. All other BA, Accounting and BS, Accounting students may take only ONE of these two courses for elective credit.
ACCT 431: Focuses on responsibility accounting, performance measurement and evaluation, and budgeting and control in various types of organizations. Additional topics may include quantitative methods in decision making and other current issues in management accounting.
ACCT 435: Provides an in-depth study of cost management systems. Topics include activity-based management, Japanese cost management techniques, and strategic cost management.
ACCT 437: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
ACCT 441: Accounting for partnerships, accounting for business combinations, parent-subsidiary consolidations, and foreign currency exchange.
ACCT 443: This course develops accounting research competence using the FASB Accounting Standards Codification (ASC). The ASC is the primary authority for all accounting measurement and reporting matters. Written and oral communications are emphasized to develop skills necessary for a professional career in accounting.
ACCT 444: Study of reporting issues from a management perspective. Introduction to the tools and techniques of financial statement analysis. Use of financial statements by external and internal decision makers. Emphasis on the development of communication and computer skills.
ACCT 447: An examination of accounting and financial reporting in governmental and not-for-profit entities and an introduction to the use of accounting information in the management of these organizations.
ACCT 451: Analysis of accounting for multinationals; area studies of accounting and financial reporting standards; and an evaluation of the international accounting harmonization effort.
ACCT 461: A study of the role of auditing and auditors in corporate financial reporting, and the importance of this role to the public. Topics covered include the audit planning process, audit reports, professional standards, and the legal and ethical responsibilities of auditors to their clients, the accounting profession and to the public.
ACCT 462: In-depth exposure to a variety of aspects of the theory and practice of professional auditing. Topics may include auditing theory and research, economic function of audits, professional standards and malpractice, new auditing techniques and services. Cases, readings, individual research, and discussion.
ACCT 466: This course examines many different aspects of fraud: what it is and the types of people more likely to commit it, how to recognize the symptoms of fraud, and how to investigate it. As such, the course will focus on topics such as internal control, financial reporting fraud, fraud detection and deterrence.
ACCT 470: Legal principles underlying the law of contracts, sales, secured transactions, real property security, bankruptcy and suretyship.
ACCT 475: Taxation of corporations and partnerships. Advanced topics in tax planning and compliance.
ACCT 477: An in-depth look at tax research and tax planning. Students will gain proficiency in tax research and apply this skill to a variety of federal taxation issues and case studies.
ACCT 479: An introduction to estates and trusts for accounting students. Course material will include: introduction to estate and trust terminology, legal aspects of wills, estates, trusts, and taxation of estates and trusts.
ACCT 484: An in-depth analysis of accounting for the natural environment. Readings, discussion and case analyses cover current issues, such as financial reporting and disclosure, management decision making and evaluation techniques, taxation and the profession's role in environmental issues.
ACCT 488: An advanced course in valuation in the small business merger and acquisition field for accounting students.
ACCT 490: Practical application of academic curriculum beyond that contained in normal undergraduate course work. Internship may not be substituted for a required or elective accounting course.
ACCT 491: Accounting or concentration-related employment, research, or special project experience. Emphasis on applying accounting or concentration principles in an academically guided setting. Minimum requirements include reflection on obtaining the internship, a work log, a comprehensive final written report, and presentation. Repeatable to a maximum of 4 credits, including original course.
ACCT 497: CBE mjr; ACCT 341; min 2.75 GPA in 300/400-lvl ACCT crses; intrnshp coordnatr apprvl
ACCT 497B: The course examines economic, environmental, and social reporting principles currently outside traditional accounting models.
AECI 301: The initial course in the Arts Enterprise and Cultural Innovation (AECI) minor sequence. This course develops the foundational tools and best practices to be used in creative self, team and project leadership, with an accomplished creative practice at the core of the enterprise. Includes overview of personality theory, research on the creative personality, and stakeholder analysis and mapping to develop effective, creative self and team leadership skills.
AECI 302: The second course in the Arts Enterprise and Cultural Innovation (AECI) minor sequence. This course explores emergent leadership models and builds on the previous course to develop leadership within networked and distributed organizations and groups. Frameworks of collaboration and creative conflict are explored to give function to the activity within a creative enterprise.
AECI 303: The third course in the Arts Enterprise and Cultural Innovation (AECI) minor sequence. Frameworks for arts organization formation and financing are explored. This course will enable creative leaders to measure the financial standing of an enterprise, test ideas and assumptions from a fiduciary perspective and fund and market projects and practices using contemporary frameworks and best practices.
AECI 304: Supervised work experience wherein the student makes an embedded contribution to a recognized formal creative enterprise under the direction and supervision of qualified practitioners. Student or program facilitated, experiential, applied learning opportunity. Existing internship experiences as defined within a CFPA major are applicable (eg. design internships).
AECI 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
AECI 405: The fourth course in the Arts Enterprise and Cultural Innovation (AECI) minor sequence. Iteration, emergent strategy, design thinking and discovery-driven growth are established as guiding frameworks for arts organizations, projects and artists. Students will understand how these frameworks operate, how to select a framework for a given situation, and how to implement the appropriate framework in ambiguous, real world circumstances.
AECI 406: The fifth course in the Arts Enterprise and Cultural Innovation (AECI) minor sequence. Disruption in the context of the creative enterprise is the result of a highly creative initiative that achieves a rift in the existing market patterns and results in a deep penetration and resonance with the audience. This course examines the frameworks that support creative disruption, and generate positive outcomes from disruption-initiated activity.
AECI 407: The culminating course in the Arts Enterprise and Cultural Innovation (AECI) minor sequence. The Capstone Lab begins with a comprehensive exam covering critical frameworks from across the five content driven course prerequisites. After completing the exam, students will develop a project or practice and take it through the process of evaluating it in terms of risk and uncertainty, building a basic business model, developing an emergent strategy, and following a design thinking process to solve problems.
AHE 375: An introduction to the study of diversity issues within the context of services and programs in higher education. Emphasis on the relationship between growth in diversity of students and the range and complexity of services and programs designed to ensure their academic and personal success.
AHE 500: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply.
AHE 501: This course focuses on understanding empirical research in the Adult and Higher Education field. In addition to examining the role and benefits of empirical research in the discipline, the course will explore the fundamentals and distinctions between quantitative and qualitative research, the importance of engaging in ethical research, and the basics of instrument design.
AHE 518: Examination and discussion of several current and controversial issues in education. Repeatable to a maximum of 12 credits, including original course.
AHE 554: This course is an introduction to the understanding of adult education as a discipline and a field. Topics include the scope, structure, philosophy, history, and issues related to diversity as well as other current factors influencing the practice of adult education.
AHE 555: This course will introduce students to research, theory, policy and practice related to diversity topics in the field of higher education and encourage students to develop their own understandings of historical and contemporary issues.
AHE 571: This course focuses on fundamental research and program evaluation methods relevant to the Adult and Higher Education field; this includes understanding the distinctions between empirical research and program evaluation. The course will provide strategies for data analysis, data visualization, and reporting out.
AHE 576: A study of contemporary theories of leadership and their application in private, public and nonprofit agencies.
AHE 577: Study of the ways adults learn and the factors related to their motivation, participation and achievement. Application of theory to practice.
AHE 580: Study and practice in teaching methodologies and assessments for adult and higher education settings. Special emphasis on facilitating student learning and applied classroom practice.
AHE 581: This is a supervised study involving readings and discussions on topics in the fields of adult education, higher education, and human services.
AHE 588: Students should be in final two quarters of the program with all required coursework completed. In this course students complete capstone projects including a portfolio of work demonstrating proficiency in AHE learning outcomes and a research proposal.
AHE 592: Field-based project is an aspect of adult and higher education to enhance theory/practice integration such as: teaching, leadership, project development, curriculum development and distance education design. Course should be taken in last year of program with most core courses already completed.
AHE 691: Graduate research under the direction of program advisor or instructor. Repeatable to a maximum of 12 credits, including original course. S/U grading.
ANTH 102: Description of scientific evidence for the evolution of the human lineage from its primitive primate ancestors to the origins of civilization. Emphasis on analytical methods employed to reconstruct history from fossils, geological context and cultural remains.
ANTH 104: The study of the cultures of the United States from the perspectives of ethnicity, race, gender and class. Special emphasis on anthropological methods and approaches to enhance understanding of contemporary socio-cultural lifeways.
ANTH 201: Introduction to the concepts, methods and practical application of cultural anthropology. The focus is on explanations for social and cultural variation around the world and over time and the significance of holistic and comparative understanding.
ANTH 210: The historical roots and current goals of archaeology. Principles of archaeological inference, including formation of the archaeological record, data collection and analysis, and interpretive frameworks.
ANTH 215: The biological side of anthropology; human osteology, primate paleontology, human variation, human evolution and primate behavior.
ANTH 247: The study of language from an anthropological perspective. Includes an introduction to the structure and patterning of language, the study of language as it is used in daily life, and the role of language in human evolution.
ANTH 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ANTH 301: The development of anthropological thought from the late 1800s to the present. Emphasis is placed on the major theoretical developments in the discipline.
ANTH 303: This course will familiarize students with perspectives, methods and techniques of qualitative research in anthropology. The course will cover the theoretical background of qualitative research, major research traditions, methods of data collection, analysis of textual data and the write-up of findings.
ANTH 308: The archaeological remains of hunting-gathering groups from early hominids to modern times interpreted in terms of evolution of adaptive strategies. Relationship to agriculture as an adaptive strategy; contributions of studies of modern hunter-gatherer groups.
ANTH 310: Village agricultural societies as revealed by archaeology; crystallization of village farming societies into urban civilizations in the Near East, Egypt, India, China and New World parallel developments.
ANTH 312: On-site training in methods and techniques of archaeological survey and excavation.
ANTH 314: Origins of PaleoIndians of North America, their paleoenvironments and the cultural sequences leading to the historic peoples of the New World north of Panama. Mesoamerican and Mississippian cultures, those of the Southwest and the Woodland Archaic.
ANTH 316: This course provides an introduction to the study of the Prehispanic civilizations of the New World. The curriculum will cover pertinent archaeological, ethnohistoric, and epigraphic data from three of the best-known new world states: the Maya of southern Mesoamerica, the Aztecs of central Mexico, and the Inca of the Andes. The perspective of this course is explicitly comparative, and case studies will be examined within the framework of anthropological theories of ancient states. For each civilization, we will examine several categories of variability, including: environmental setting, origins of complexity, political organization, social organization, economy, and religion and ideology.
ANTH 320: Training in osteology, bioarchaeology and evolutionary biology. Critical reading and discussion of scientific literature that deals with the biological and biocultural interpretation of the human skeletal record, focusing on occult themes. Topics include mummies, cannibals, vampires, paleopathology, mystical sites (ie Stonehenge), and more.
ANTH 323: Discussion of concepts in human evolutionary biology and biological anthropology as presented in American science-fiction literature. Topics include human migration, gene exchange, coexistence of hominid species, human variation and the fallacy of the binary, technology and natural selection, and the future of our species.
ANTH 325: The biology and anthropology of human reproduction, physiology, and anatomy. Critical reading and discussion of scientific literature that deals with the biological and biocultural history of reproduction and physiology, focusing on modern humans. Topics include reproductive anatomy, sex and gender, fertility, demography, the obstetrical ‘dilemma’, and the evolution of pregnancy.
ANTH 330: Comparative study of religious thought, belief and behavior; relationship of religious experience and institutions to other aspects of culture and society.
ANTH 335: Mathematics and statistics as applied to anthropological problems.
ANTH 338: Examines the relationship between systems of production and culture through four theoretical approaches: formalist, substantivist, Marxist and culturalist. Emphasis on localized consequences of global economic forces. Service learning component required.
ANTH 345: Energy has played a key role in the sociocultural and economic transformation of the Global South. This class examines the historical dimensions of these energy projects as a central component of modernization and national development. It also explores the impact on communities around the world of new or alternative energy technologies, infrastructures, politics, and political alliances, especially in light of the challenges presented by global climate change. Also offered as ENRG 345.
ANTH 347: Familiarizes students with methods of data collection and analysis used in linguistic anthropology through an examination of both classic and current literature. Examines the complex relationship between language and culture.
ANTH 350: Examines global contemporary sociopolitical, health and related environmental issues with an evolutionary perspective that emphasizes changes in human physiology, development, and the genome and epigenome relative to local ecology (disease, diet, demography) and cultural adaptations.
ANTH 353: Cross-cultural study of gender stereotypes, gender and language, gender and work roles, gender and religion.
ANTH 361: In this course, we will define the concepts of colonialism and Indigeneity, and explore how Indigenous peoples' daily life and cultural experiences have been shaped by these political systems. Students will examine the colonial legacies of the discipline of anthropology, read works by Indigenous anthropologists and scholars, and put local experiences of Indigeneity and colonialism in a broader context across North America and the globe.
ANTH 362: Ethnographic survey of the region, with attention to the diversity of human experience.
ANTH 365: Ethnographic survey of the region, with attention to the diversity of human experience.
ANTH 366: Ethnographic survey of the region, with attention to the diversity of human experience.
ANTH 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ANTH 406: History of theory and method in North American archaeology and the legacy of earlier goals. Current goals and the development of appropriate theory, method and empirical applications.
ANTH 410: Archaeological laboratory methods; artifact identification, classification, measurement; map reproduction, soil and feature profiles; use of photographs and other graphic methods.
ANTH 411: The prehistoric archaeology of the Northwest coast and plateaus; current explorations and interpretations in a context of paleoenvironmental and ethnohistorical evidence.
ANTH 415: Focuses on the application of advanced quantitative methods in spatial analysis to specific archaeological contexts and projects. Students will complete a major research project and present it to the class and as a paper.
ANTH 420: After learning the human skeleton, the student will be trained in techniques for recovery of the body, reconstruction of the body's history (age, sex, race, etc.) and how to aid the crime investigator.
ANTH 422: The study of human nutrition and diet from an anthropological perspective. Topics include the structure and function of the digestive system, the chemical composition of nutrients and the regulation by the body of nutrient stores and body composition. Focuses on using a comparative approach to understand the evolution of human diet, and the impacts of technology and culture on modern nutrition.
ANTH 423: First half of seminar covers theory and anatomical changes for hominid species focusing on last 6 million years (that is, Ardipithecus and Australopithecus to present) and second half considers sociocultural evolution (e.g., life history theory, mate choice, evolution of cognition, emotions, language).
ANTH 424: Introduction to an area where biological and cultural anthropology interface. Includes health and disease in evolution, the relationships between disease and world view, the healer and the cultural milieu, and comparative studies of healing practices.
ANTH 426: This course examines patterns of human genetic variation, characterizing the concepts of inheritance, gene expression, the relationship of genotype to phenotype and the growing role of epigenetics in human development, adaptation and evolution.
ANTH 428: Introduction to the field of cultural resource management including historic preservation, archaeological resource management, cultural resource management for subsistence and spiritual practices. Background on legislation and current practices, review of case studies and experience with actual projects.
ANTH 431: Future generations face the challenge of developing sufficient and sustainable nutritional provisions to feed the global population. Technology, climate change, massive migrations, environmental contamination and politics all compel us to elucidate the efficacy of resulting changes to our food chain and their subsequent biological outcome. Using a nutritional epidemiology approach, this course is designed to learn from past research mistakes resulting in misguided nutritional policies and to develop skills needed to design anthropological research strategies for nutritional studies for the 21st Century.
ANTH 437: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
ANTH 437G: The program consists of an intensive seven-week service learning field course with an academic focus on Balinese and Timorese culture, ecology and adaptations to climate change. In the course students will develop skills in field based participant observation, language skills, recording field notes, water quality sampling and ethnographic writing. With ANTH advisor approval, students may substitute this course for ANTH 463 or ANTH 471/480 for ANTH degree requirements.
ANTH 440: The interdisciplinary field of Science and Technology Studies explores the cultures of science production, the experience of technology in our lives, and the values, ethics, policies, and politics of science and tech. This course examines how anthropology contributes to understanding human experiences in relation to the material and ideological conditions of our technological age.
ANTH 447: Myth, metaphor and media offer the material for this exploration of theories which offer insight into the relationship between language and mind.
ANTH 453: Explores women's economic, religious, political and familial roles through topics such as development and globalization, violence, and women's movements. Student contributions to course topics emphasized through individual papers and group panel work. Also offered as WGSS 453.
ANTH 454: Collaborative and community-engaged research involves using methods, such as Participatory Action Research and collaborative ethnography, to work alongside community members to develop actionable research by co-developing research questions, conducting research, and analyzing and applying findings. In this course, students will work with identified community members and organizations to practice research conducted with and in community.
ANTH 455: In this course, students will practice conducting ethnographic research, a core method in anthropology. Course work will include designing ethnographic research questions, engaging in participant observation, taking field notes, conducting interviews, using qualitative data analysis software, and developing an ethnographic research product.
ANTH 456: The course focuses on emic and etic perspectives of war and human rights. Investigates cultural relativism and anthropology with regard to war and violence. Cultural constructions of war and definitions of human rights are fundamental to an understanding of what it means to be human.
ANTH 457: The course considers death and dying anthropologically as cultural constructs. The course explores a wide range of cultures from a variety of interdisciplinary and interactive perspectives in order to further our understanding of what it means to be human. Studies death and dying in order to broaden our understanding of the human cultural experience. Field trips required.
ANTH 462: Tribal distributions, social organization and ecological adaptation and social change with emphasis on the Indigenous peoples of Washington state.
ANTH 463: An ethnographic in-depth study of the national and minority peoples of China, mainland and insular Southeast Asia. Emphasis on special topics, including ecology, prehistory and selected cultural groups. Readings focus on original monographs.
ANTH 465: Examination of contemporary issues in the southern part of North America, with emphasis on changing cultural, political, and environmental contexts; urban, rural, and indigenous communities; migration and transcultural realities; and social and environmental movements.
ANTH 469: Application of anthropological methods and theory in an applied setting. Interns work at least 10 hours per week at the work site, in the type of work specified in the internship contract. In addition students complete several written assignments, Repeatable to a maximum of 15 credits. No more than 10 credits in internship may be counted toward the major.
ANTH 470: Internship at the Whatcom Museum of History and Art or other local museums. Students may select an area of museum specialization in most cases; essay questions and a paper are also required. Repeatable to a maximum of 10 credits, including original course. This course has been approved for study abroad.
ANTH 472: Examination of photographic representation of people by anthropologists, ethnographic filmmakers, indigenous people, media and other groups. Analytical skills and applications are emphasized and theoretical perspectives are explored.
ANTH 476: Comparative examination of simultaneous separating and integrating functions of borders, significance of border regions as vital transition zones, and transboundary policy needs associated with accelerated flows of people, goods and ideas; particular focus on U.S.-Mexico and US.-Canada borderlands.
ANTH 479: This is an internship at the Whatcom Museum, specifically to prepare students for workshops/tours for a program titled The People of the Sea and Cedar, which focuses on Northwest Coast Native peoples. The student will conduct workshops/tours for third and fourth grade students studying Native American history and culture. Interns will also learn about broader museum topics through readings and demonstrate their understandings through weekly short essays. A self-evaluation and Summary of Learning is also required. Interns should be comfortable working with people and hold an interest in Native American culture. Interns will need to be available for certain hours and make a two consecutive quarter commitment. Repeatable up to 7 credits including original course.
ANTH 480: Use of anthropology to solve human problems; examines ethics, interventions and policy applications regarding contemporary social issues.
ANTH 481: The process of socialization or enculturation viewed from a cross-cultural perspective.
ANTH 490: Capstone seminar in anthropology. Topics vary, emphasis is on current research questions in anthropology. Students write a research proposal, conduct a research project and present the findings. Repeatable to a maximum of 10 credits.
ANTH 495: Practicum as discussion leaders in anthropology courses. May be repeated once for departmental credit if taken from a different instructor.
ANTH 496: Student assembles and submits portfolio contents in four areas: research, competence, data analysis, critical comprehension and synthetic comparison, under continuing direction of departmental academic adviser. S/U grading.
ANTH 500: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply.
ANTH 501: Development of principal theoretical orientations and methods in the cultural and historical setting; development of anthropology as a discipline.
ANTH 502: Issues relating to use of theory in contemporary anthropological research; examination of major writings and their implications.
ANTH 503: Analysis of major theoretical approaches; research methods and procedures; relationship of theory and method in formulating research problems.
ANTH 506: History of theory and method in North American archaeology and the legacy of earlier interpretive frameworks. Current goals of the discipline and the development of appropriate theory, method and empirical applications.
ANTH 510: Advanced design and implementation of archaeological laboratory methods to a specific research project.
ANTH 511: Advanced survey of current literature in Pacific Northwest archaeology in seminar format with preparation of a major research paper.
ANTH 515: Application of advanced quantitative spatial analysis techniques to specific archaeological contexts and projects. Students will complete a major research project and paper.
ANTH 520: Advanced study of human osteology. The latest methods in reconstruction of the individual.
ANTH 522: Advanced study of human nutrition and metabolism from an anthropological perspective. Topics include the structure and function of the digestive system, the chemical composition of nutrients and the regulation by the body of nutrient stores and body composition. Each student will prepare a major research paper and presentation.
ANTH 524: Advanced study of the use of medical anthropological method and theory in contemporary health care systems or in the analysis of health and disease in past populations.
ANTH 525: Advanced study of primate paleontology. Each student is expected to become expert on some aspect of the fossil record.
ANTH 526: Advanced study to examine patterns of human genetic variation, characterizing the concepts of inheritance, gene expression, the relationship of genotype to phenotype and the growing role epigenetics in human development, adaptation and evolution.
ANTH 528: Application of cultural resource management methods to specific management problems. Students will prepare a professional quality cultural resource management plan or nomination form.
ANTH 531: Future generations face the challenge of developing sufficient and sustainable nutritional provisions to feed the global population. Technology, climate change, massive migrations, environmental contamination and politics all compel us to elucidate the efficacy of resulting changes to our food chain and their subsequent biological outcome. Using a nutritional epidemiology approach, this course is designed to learn from past research mistakes resulting in misguided nutritional policies and to develop skills needed to design anthropological research strategies for nutritional studies for the 21st Century.
ANTH 547: Advanced study of theoretical approaches to meaning in linguistic anthropology, including but not limited to Piercean semiotics, trope theory, and methods for theorizing context.
ANTH 553: Examines a variety of contemporary issues facing women of the South, such as economic realities, family responsibilities, health issues, and women's rights. Emphasis on individual and group work to examine selected topics and to gain in-depth knowledge about women in specific countries.
ANTH 554: Collaborative and community-engaged research involves using methods, such as Participatory Action Research and collaborative ethnography, to work alongside community members to develop actionable research by co-developing research questions, conducting research, and analyzing and applying findings. In this course, students will work with identified community members and organizations to practice research conducted with and in community.
ANTH 555: In this course, students will practice conducting ethnographic research, a core method in anthropology. Course work will include designing ethnographic research questions, engaging in participant observation, taking field notes, conducting interviews, using qualitative data analysis software, and developing an ethnographic research product.
ANTH 563: Advanced study of selected important topics regarding the peoples and cultures of China, mainland and insular Southeast Asia. Emphasis on work to gain in-depth knowledge and understanding of selected cultures and/or theoretical-analytical topics of special relevance to the region.
ANTH 565: Advanced ethnological analysis of cultures and social relations in Mesoamerica, with emphasis on ecological, economic and political issues and implications for community resources for facing globalization.
ANTH 572: Examination of photographic/digital image representation of people by anthropologists, ethnographic filmmakers, indigenous people, media and other groups. Requires analytical skills and applications and explores theoretical perspectives. Requires two projects with accompanying presentations.
ANTH 576: Advanced comparative examination of separating and integrating functions of borders, border regions as transition zones, and policy implications, with emphasis on U.S. borders with Mexico and Canada.
ANTH 580: Advanced investigation of the use of anthropology to solve human problems; ethics, interventions and policy applications regarding contemporary social issues.
ANTH 581: Advanced cultural analysis of the process of socialization, child welfare and policy relating to children.
ANTH 585: This course will acquaint students with faculty interests and departmental and university resources. Topics will include choosing a thesis research topic aligned with contemporary issues in anthropology, forming a committee, and developing an appropriate plan of study. S/U grading.
ANTH 586: A seminar style class to discuss progress and issues in thesis development at various stages: writing a thesis topic proposal, submitting grant proposals and IRB proposals, and the logistics of conducting research. Other topics will include standards for professional writing and giving professional presentations. Students will be expected to present their thesis proposal in this venue. Repeatable for a minimum of 3 and maximum of 5 credits.
ANTH 690: Repeatable to a maximum of 12 cr. S/U grading

ARAB 102: 101, 102, 103 Elementary Arabic (5 each). To be taken in sequence. Fundamentals of speaking, reading, writing and understanding standard Arabic.
